screens.title: Setting Up Your React Native Development Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will build a reliable foundation for React Native development. We'll explain why Node. js is required, how npm and yarn manage the libraries your projects depend on, and why Expo CLI is an efficient way to start without touching native toolchains. You will also learn when to use the React Native CLI, what a simulator and the Expo Go app do, and which editor and extensions help you debug as you learn. I'll guide you through concrete commands to create and run your first Expo project, and point out common pitfalls like forgetting to install global tools or mixing Node versions. By the end of the chapter you'll know how to install the core tools, start a development server, open the app on a device or emulator, and fix the usual setup problems that block newcomers. Keep an eye out for simple checks you can run right away to confirm your environment is correct.

Setting Up Your React Native Development Environment

Install Node.js and a package manager, choose Expo for fast prototyping, and learn the essentials of running and debugging your first app on a device or simulator.

Node.js → package manager → Expo or RN CLI → device/simulator

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this first set of objectives you'll focus on identifying and installing the core tools for React Native. You will learn what Node. js provides, how npm and yarn control dependencies, and the commands to install global CLI tools safely. I will describe concrete examples like installing yarn via npm and what the global flag changes. These skills let you prepare a machine that can run, build, and share JavaScript code for mobile apps. We will also practice a quick check so you can verify the major tools are available after installation. A common misconception is that any random version of Node will work; we explain how mismatched Node versions can cause installation errors and how to avoid that by using a version manager. By the end of this screen you will know the reasons for each tool, a command to install them, and a short test you can run to confirm success.

screens.title: Node.js: the JavaScript runtime you need
screens.narratorSegment: Node. js is the JavaScript runtime that lets JavaScript run on your computer outside the browser. In practice this means the build tools, package managers, bundlers, and development servers React Native relies on all run on Node. A concrete example: when you run the Expo development server, Node executes the server process that bundles your JavaScript and serves it to the Expo Go app. One common misconception is thinking that the mobile device needs Node installed: it does not. The device receives the JavaScript bundle your computer produces. Another frequent issue is using incompatible Node versions which can cause package installation errors; use a version manager if you need multiple versions. Example check: run the runtime command to see its version and confirm it is installed. Key takeaway: Node is the foundation that runs the tools you use to develop, not the app on the device itself. Reflect: if your install fails, confirm Node is present and at a supported version before moving on. Node.js: the JavaScript runtime you need means node runs the dev server and installers — without it, the react native toolchain cannot execute.. In practical terms, what node provides and why react native depends on it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept

Node.js — runtime explained

Node.js runs JavaScript on your machine so development tools like bundlers, package managers, and dev servers can execute. It is not required on the mobile device that runs the app.

Definition: A server-side JavaScript runtime used by tooling.
Example: expo start runs a Node process that serves your JavaScript bundle.
Misconception: You do not need Node on your phone; only on your development machine.
Key Takeaway

Install Node first and confirm the version to avoid later tooling issues.

Quick checks and example
node --version
# expected output example: v14.17.0
If the command prints a version, Node is installed. If not, install Node.js before proceeding.
Analogy
Think of Node as the engine that runs your build tools; without it, the car won’t move even if the rest is assembled.

screens.title: Package Managers: npm and Yarn
screens.narratorSegment: Package managers install and manage the JavaScript libraries your project needs. npm is bundled with Node, and yarn is an alternative many developers prefer for speed and deterministic installs. A central idea is the difference between local and global installs. Local installs add a package to a specific project's dependencies so it can be imported by your code. Global installs make a tool available in your shell, which is appropriate for CLI tools like the Expo CLI. A common beginner mistake is using the project install command when intending to install a global tool. For example, using yarn add will install a package locally; to install globally with yarn you run yarn global add expo-cli. With npm, the corresponding global flag is npm install -g expo-cli. Try the commands and verify the global binary is available. Misconception check: global installs do not add the package to the project dependencies. Takeaway: choose the correct command for the scope you want and confirm with a version check. Package Managers: npm and Yarn means use local installs for dependencies; use global installs for cli tools and confirm with a version check.. In practical terms, what they do, global vs local installs, and correct global commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Local vs Global
keyIdea.text: Use local installs for dependencies; use global installs for CLI tools and confirm with a version check.

content.html:
Definition

npm vs Yarn

Both install packages. npm ships with Node. yarn is an alternative package manager you can install using npm and then use to manage dependencies with consistent locking.

Local install example: npm install react-native — adds to project dependencies.
Global install example: npm install -g expo-cli — makes the CLI available system-wide.
Common mistake: using yarn add when you intended a global install.
Commands (try these in your terminal)
# Install yarn using npm
npm install -g yarn

# Install Expo CLI globally with npm
npm install -g expo-cli

# Or with yarn
yarn global add expo-cli

# Verify versions
node --version
npm --version
yarn --version
After installation, confirm the global binary is present by checking its version. If you see an error, you may have installed without the global flag or need permission adjustments.

screens.title: Using Expo CLI to create and run a project
screens.narratorSegment: Expo CLI simplifies creating and running a React Native app without configuring native toolchains. The typical flow is: install the Expo CLI globally, create a new project with an init command selecting a blank template, navigate into the project folder, and start the development server. Expo produces a QR code which the Expo Go app can scan to load your app on a physical device. Alternatively, you can open an Android emulator or iOS simulator using terminal keys if the required native tooling exists. A concrete example: running expo init HelloReactNative creates a starter project, and npm start or expo start launches the dev server. Common mistakes include not installing the CLI globally and attempting to scan a QR code when the phone is not on the same network as your computer. Key takeaway: Expo lets you focus on JavaScript and UI iteration, and the dev server with live reload is the immediate feedback loop you need to learn quickly. Using Expo CLI to create and run a project means expo init → expo start → scan qr or press emulator keys to see live changes rapidly.. In practical terms, init, start, and open on a device or simulator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow

Create and run with Expo

1
Install Expo CLI
npm install -g expo-cli
2
Create a project
expo init HelloReactNative (choose blank)
3
Start the dev server
npm start or expo start — scan the QR or press a/i for emulators
Key Takeaway

Expo gives you a fast feedback loop so you can focus on building UI in JavaScript.

Terminal demo (commands)
# Install Expo CLI globally
npm install -g expo-cli

# Create a new project using the blank template
expo init HelloReactNative

# Change into the project and start
cd HelloReactNative
npm start
When the server starts it prints a QR code in the terminal and opens the Expo Dev Tools in a browser. Scan with Expo Go to run on a device, or press 'a' or 'i' in the terminal to launch emulators when configured.

screens.title: Your First Expo React Native Project — Step-by-step
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through creating and modifying a small Expo app so you can see live reload in action. First install the Expo CLI globally if you haven't already. Then run expo init HelloReactNative and choose the blank template. Change into the created folder and run npm start. When the dev server runs, it serves a QR code the Expo Go app can scan; if you prefer, press a to open an Android emulator or i to open an iOS simulator when available. Next, open the project in Visual Studio Code, find App. js, and change the displayed text in the main Text element to a short greeting. Save the file and watch the app update instantly in Expo Go or the simulator. A common misconception is that you need to rebuild the native app to see simple JavaScript changes; with Expo and live reload, most UI tweaks appear immediately. Takeaway: this rapid feedback loop is the core of iterative mobile development. keyIdea.text: Modify App.js, save, and observe instant updates in Expo Go or a simulator without rebuilding native code.

content.html:
Hands-on

Create and edit

Follow the commands to make a project, then edit App.js to replace the starter text with a personalized message to confirm live reload works.

Command: expo init HelloReactNative
Command: cd HelloReactNative
Command: npm start
Key Takeaway

A single file edit and save should update the app immediately when the dev server is running.

Example App.js change
import React from 'react';
import { Text, View } from 'react-native';

export default function App() {
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, alignItems: 'center', justifyContent: 'center' }}>
      <Text>Hello, Cohortia React Native!</Text>
    </View>
  );
}
Replace the Text content, save, and the updated text should appear immediately in Expo Go or your simulator. If it doesn't, check the dev server output for errors or a blocked port.

screens.title: Expo managed workflow vs React Native CLI bare workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Expo's managed workflow wraps many native details so you can write JavaScript and preview on devices quickly. It is ideal for learning, prototypes, and many app types where custom native modules aren't required. The React Native CLI bare workflow gives you direct access to native Xcode and Android Studio projects, which is necessary when you must add or modify native code. A concrete scenario: if you need a custom native library not supported by Expo, you will use the bare workflow and open the native projects in Xcode or Android Studio. A common misconception is believing Expo cannot ever use native modules — Expo can support certain native code through a workflow called 'eject' but that moves you toward the bare workflow. Key contrast: Expo increases speed and simplicity; React Native CLI increases control and complexity. Takeaway: start with Expo for speed, and consider the bare workflow only when a specific native need arises. Expo managed workflow vs React Native CLI bare workflow means choose expo for fast iteration; choose the react native cli when custom native code is required.. In practical terms, when to prototype quickly and when to work with native projects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Speed vs control
keyIdea.text: Choose Expo for fast iteration; choose the React Native CLI when custom native code is required.

content.html:
Comparison
Expo Managed Workflow
Pros: fast setup, no native IDE required, quick device testing with Expo Go. Cons: limited direct native access unless you eject.
React Native CLI (Bare)
Pros: full native control and ability to add custom native modules. Cons: requires Xcode and Android Studio setup, more configuration work.
Scenario example
You are building an app that needs access to a proprietary native SDK not supported by Expo. In that case you would choose the React Native CLI bare workflow to integrate the SDK directly into the native iOS and Android projects.
Misconception
Ejecting from Expo is a migration step toward the bare workflow; it is possible but requires more setup and management of native projects.
Key Takeaway

Start with Expo to prototype quickly; move to the bare workflow when you need direct native capabilities.

screens.title: The development toolchain architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the toolchain architecture helps you see where each problem can appear. The chain starts with Node running local tooling. Package managers install libraries into your project. The Expo CLI or React Native CLI runs a bundler and development server that packages your JavaScript into a bundle. The device or emulator receives that bundle either through the Expo Go app or the native runtime when using the bare workflow. A practical example: when your app fails to load in Expo Go, the root cause could be an interrupted dev server (Node process), a package misinstall, or a network problem preventing the device from reaching the dev server. A helpful troubleshooting approach is to run a simple sequence of checks: confirm Node is running, check the dev server output, verify the device can reach the host, and ensure dependencies installed successfully. Misconception: the device runs its own build of your source; in most Expo cases it runs the JavaScript bundle served by your machine. Takeaway: follow the chain to find where failures occur. The development toolchain architecture means trace problems from node → package manager → dev server → device to isolate failures quickly.. In practical terms, how node, package managers, expo, simulators and devices fit together. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Architecture

Toolchain components

Node.js (runtime)
npm / yarn (package manager)
Expo CLI / RN CLI (dev server)
Device / Simulator receives the JavaScript bundle served by the dev server.
Example check sequence: confirm Node version, run the dev server, look for bundler errors, ensure device is reachable and on the same network, then reload the app.
Practical scenario
If the app does not load in Expo Go, ask: is the dev server running? Are dependencies installed? Is the computer and device on the same network? This systematic approach isolates the failure point quickly.
Key Takeaway

Map the flow from tool to device and check each step to find the source of errors effectively.

screens.title: Setting up native tools: Xcode and Android Studio
screens.narratorSegment: Xcode and Android Studio are native IDEs required for building and running full native projects and emulators. For Expo managed projects you generally do not need them to iterate, but the React Native CLI requires Xcode for iOS builds and Android Studio for Android builds and emulators. Installing Xcode on Mac O S is typically done through the Mac App Store and includes the iOS simulator. Android Studio requires downloading SDKs, configuring environment variables, and creating virtual devices for emulation. A common trap is starting a bare workflow project without the native tools installed; that will prevent you from building the native apps. Another misconception is that installing Android Studio alone is sufficient — you must also configure SDK platforms and create an AVD (Android Virtual Device). Key takeaway: only install these heavy tools when you need native-level capabilities; otherwise, Expo accelerates development without them. Definition

Xcode and Android Studio

Xcode provides the iOS toolchain and simulator on macOS. Android Studio provides the Android SDK, tools, and virtual devices. Both are required for building native binaries and deep native debugging when using the bare workflow.

Install Xcode from the Mac App Store to get the iOS simulator (macOS only).
Install Android Studio and configure SDK platforms and an AVD to run Android emulators.
Common pitfall: starting a bare project without these tools prevents native builds from compiling.
When to install
If you are only experimenting with UI and JavaScript logic, stick with Expo. Install native toolchains when you must integrate or build native modules or create release binaries.

Avoid the heavy native installs until you need them; they increase setup time and complexity.

screens.title: Common setup issues and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: When setup fails, the same few issues appear repeatedly. First, forgetting the global flag when installing a CLI commonly results in a missing command. Troubleshooting

Checklist for setup issues

  • Confirm CLI installed globally and accessible via the terminal.
  • Check Node and package manager versions; use a version manager if needed.
  • Verify device and computer share a network and that firewall rules are not blocking traffic.
Common Mistake

Running a project without a global CLI install or with the wrong Node version is the most frequent blocker.

Repair commands and checks
# Reinstall Expo CLI globally
npm install -g expo-cli

# Use a version manager (example placeholder)
# nvm install 14 && nvm use 14

# Restart dev server
npm start
After running these checks, review the dev server logs for hints and retry connecting your device. If network errors persist, try a different network or tethering to isolate the issue.

screens.narratorSegment: Editing App. js and watching the change appear on your device is one of the most immediate proofs that your environment works.
